verses.text: In the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel had come out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build Yahweh’s house.
The house which king Solomon built for Yahweh had a length of sixty cubits,  and its width twenty, and its height thirty cubits.
The porch in front of the temple of the house had a length of twenty cubits, which was along the width of the house. Ten cubits was its width in front of the house.
He made windows of fixed lattice work for the house.
Against the wall of the house, he built floors all around, against the walls of the house all around, both of the temple and of the inner sanctuary; and he made side rooms all around.

The lowest floor was five cubits wide, and the middle was six cubits wide, and the third was seven cubits wide; for on the outside he made offsets in the wall of the house all around, that the beams should not be inserted into the walls of the house.
The house, when it was under construction, was built of stone prepared at the quarry; and no hammer or ax or any tool of iron was heard in the house while it was under construction.
The door for the middle side rooms was in the right side of the house. They went up by winding stairs into the middle floor, and out of the middle into the third.
So he built the house, and finished it; and he covered the house with beams and planks of cedar.
He built the floors all along the house, each five cubits high; and they rested on the house with timber of cedar.
Yahweh’s word came to Solomon, saying,

“Concerning this house which you are building, if you will walk in my statutes, and execute my ordinances, and keep all my commandments to walk in them; then I will establish my word with you, which I spoke to David your father.
I will dwell among the children of Israel, and will not forsake my people Israel.”
So Solomon built the house, and finished it.

He built the walls of the house within with boards of cedar: from the floor of the house to the walls of the ceiling, he covered them on the inside with wood; and he covered the floor of the house with cypress boards.
He built twenty cubits on the back part of the house with boards of cedar from the floor to the ceiling. He built them for it within, for an inner sanctuary, even for the most holy place.
In front of the temple sanctuary was forty cubits.
There was cedar on the house within, carved with buds and open flowers. All was cedar. No stone was visible.
He prepared an inner sanctuary in the middle of the house within, to set the ark of Yahweh’s covenant there.
Within the inner sanctuary was twenty cubits in length, and twenty cubits in width, and twenty cubits in its height; and he overlaid it with pure gold; and he covered the altar with cedar.
So Solomon overlaid the house within with pure gold. He drew chains of gold across before the inner sanctuary, and he overlaid it with gold.
He overlaid the whole house with gold, until all the house was finished. He also overlaid the whole altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary with gold.
In the inner sanctuary he made two cherubim  of olive wood, each ten cubits high.
Five cubits was the one wing of the cherub, and five cubits the other wing of the cherub. From the tip of one wing to the tip of the other was ten cubits.
The other cherub was ten cubits. Both the cherubim were of one measure and one form.
One cherub was ten cubits high, and so was the other cherub.

He set the cherubim within the inner house. The wings of the cherubim were stretched out, so that the wing of the one touched the one wall, and the wing of the other cherub touched the other wall; and their wings touched one another in the middle of the house.
He overlaid the cherubim with gold.
He carved all the walls of the house around with carved figures of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, inside and outside.
He overlaid the floor of the house with gold, inside and outside.
For the entrance of the inner sanctuary, he made doors of olive wood. The lintel and door posts were a fifth part of the wall.
So he made two doors of olive wood; and he carved on them carvings of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, and overlaid them with gold. He spread the gold on the cherubim and on the palm trees.
He also did so for the entrance of the temple door posts of olive wood, out of a fourth part of the wall;
and two doors of cypress wood. The two leaves of the one door were folding, and the two leaves of the other door were folding.
He carved cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers; and he overlaid them with gold fitted on the engraved work.
He built the inner court with three courses of cut stone and a course of cedar beams.
The foundation of Yahweh’s house was laid in the fourth year, in the month Ziv.
In the eleventh year, in the month Bul, which is the eighth month, the house was finished throughout all its parts, and according to all its specifications. So he spent seven years building it.

footnotes.content: Four hundred eighty years—a long journey from slavery to kingship. Solomon's fourth year marks the exact moment the work begins: not before preparation was complete, not after another delay. The Lord's house is built on His timing, not ours.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sixty cubits long, twenty wide, thirty high—vast proportions, yet exact. Every measurement matters when you're building for the Holy One. The place of God's dwelling is neither cramped nor wasteful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The porch stands before the holy place, a threshold where the ordinary meets the sacred. This is where approaching hearts pause, remembering they draw near to Yahweh.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fixed lattice work—light filters through pattern. Even in a house of cedar and gold, the Lord's dwelling allows natural light to enter in measured ways. Nothing is left to random chance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Side rooms built all around—the sanctuary is surrounded by service space. Those who serve in God's house need shelter too. The structure itself teaches that all work around the holy is part of one purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Each floor wider than the last—offsets in the wall so beams are not burdened by weight above. How like the Lord to remember that even stones need support, and strength is built wisely.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Stone dressed at the quarry, then assembled in silence—no iron sound during construction. What sacred work, that the Lord's house rises without the noise of violence. Here again, reverence shapes the method.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Winding stairs lead upward, passage after passage, growing higher toward the inner rooms. The climb itself teaches: access to God's presence is not immediate, but approached with ascending prayer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Finished and covered with cedar beams and planks—the structure is complete. I hear the exhale of the builders and, beyond that, the stillness of a house now enclosed and set apart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Each floor five cubits high, resting on timbers of cedar—strength upon strength. God's house is not hastily built but grounded in materials that endure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Right in the midst of the work, while hammers still echo and artisans labor, the Lord speaks to Solomon. He breaks in with His word—not after, but now, even as the building rises.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If you walk in My statutes, I will establish My word—this is the gospel condition beneath the stone. The house of wood and cedar is only a shelter if the One who dwells there is honored by obedience within it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I will not forsake My people Israel—the covenantal promise reaches across centuries. Even when kings fail, even when the people stumble, the Lord will not abandon His own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon finished it. The work is done, the vision complete. Yet we know from later scriptures that the building, however magnificent, could not contain the One it honored.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cedar inside, cypress underfoot—the finest woods line the inner spaces. Only the most precious materials touch the ground and walls of God's house. The craftsmanship is prayer in wood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twenty cubits behind the cedar boards—the inner sanctuary, most holy place. That is where the ark will rest, where the presence dwells. Everything built points inward and upward to that final chamber.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Forty cubits in front—space for prayer and offering, for the priests to minister. The outer sanctuary is twice the inner, yet the inner is never diminished; both have their purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cedar carved with buds and open flowers—the very wood speaks of new life, growth, beauty. No stone visible; all is wood, all is organic, all is decorated with the promise of flourishing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The inner sanctuary prepared for the ark—that chest holding the covenant tablets. Everything in this house exists to give the ark a dwelling place and to guard the holiness stored within.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A perfect cube—twenty by twenty by twenty, entirely overlaid with pure gold. The most holy place is symmetry and radiance, reflecting the perfection of the One who will be worshipped there.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gold chains drawn across before the inner sanctuary—a barrier of beauty, both protection and adornment. You cannot simply walk in; the Lord's holiness is marked and honored by this partition.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The whole house overlaid with gold until it was finished—everything unified, everything transformed into radiance. The altar itself is not stone but wood and gold, a creation fitting for the One approached there.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two cherubim of olive wood, each ten cubits high—these heavenly figures stand as guardians and witnesses. In every holy place, the unseen realm is remembered by carved images of the watchers who see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Five cubits on each side, wingspan of ten—the cherubim are vast, their arms spread wide. They are not small attendants but mighty creatures whose very proportions speak of God's grandeur.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Both cherubim of one measure and one form—matching witnesses, in perfect accord. They stand together in the sanctuary, a picture of unified praise before the throne of God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Each cherub ten cubits high—the text restates what was already told, as if to hold the image steady in our minds. These are no small carvings but monumental, towering figures of holiness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wings stretched out so each touched one wall, their wings meeting in the middle—the cherubim embrace the ark between them. Here is protection, here is the sense that God's presence is held safe by powers beyond our reckoning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The cherubim overlaid with gold—even these mighty figures are clothed in light, made radiant. Nothing in this place is left ordinary; all is transformed by the presence of the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All walls carved with cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, inside and out—the sanctuary is not bare stone but a forest of images speaking of protection, victory, and life. Every surface teaches.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The floor overlaid with gold, inside and outside—even what you walk upon is precious here. To set foot in the Lord's house is to walk on glory itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Doors of olive wood for the inner sanctuary—a threshold that marks passage from the outer holy place to the most holy. This door is not locked but closed, waiting for the high priest's approach.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers carved upon the doors—even the gate is a work of art and prayer. What you pass through to approach God is itself beautiful, inviting trust and wonder.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The temple door receives the same care—olive wood and proportioned doorposts. The entrance to the outer sanctuary is no less dignified than the inner, because all who enter seek to draw near to God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two doors of cypress wood, each with folding leaves—double doors that fold, allowing the priest to pass through. The design itself is graceful, making room for movement even at the boundary of the holy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cherubim, palm trees, and flowers again, overlaid with gold fitted on the engraved work—the pattern repeats across every entrance and surface. The decoration is not excess but consistency, one message carved and gilded everywhere.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The inner court built with cut stone and cedar beams—the courts themselves are structured with care, alternating stone and wood. The sanctuary is not built on stone alone but on stone grounded in living wood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The foundation laid in the fourth year—Yahweh's house is grounded in the earth. Even the building that will hold the holy must rest on stone and time, on patience and the Lord's purpose unfolding.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven years—a whole cycle to build the house of God. Readers today hear an echo in these years: the Lord does not rush what is sacred. When we build lives of worship, our own 'seven years' matter; patience itself is prayer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
